tip: Εσείς (esis) and the -ετε (-ete) of έχετε (ekhete) are the polite-or-plural 'you': one person you respect, or several people.
Σχολείο (skholio) goes bare: πάει σχολείο (pai skholio) has no 'to' and no 'the' – like English 'goes home', but for school.
Αυτή (afti) is 'this one' for feminine words – it matches γυναίκα (yineka = woman/wife). A neuter word would take αυτό (afto).
Του (tou = his) follows the noun: η γυναίκα του (i yineka tou), literally 'the wife his'.
Στην (stin) is σε (se) + την (tin) squeezed together: στην τσάντα (stin tsanta) = in the bag. Greek always contracts σε (se) with 'the'.
Greek 'the' changes with gender: η (i) goes with feminine words like η βαλίτσα (i valitsa = the suitcase).
Το (to) is the neuter 'the': το βιβλίο (to vivlio = the book). Στο (sto) = σε (se) + το (to), 'at the'.
Ο (o) is the masculine 'the': ο υπολογιστής (o ipoloyistis = the computer). The adjective matches too: παλιός (palios = old).
Greek has one present tense: τρώει (troi) covers both 'eats' and 'is eating'. τώρα (tora = now) supplies the -ing feel.
No 'do' helper for negation – δεν (dhen) before the verb does the whole job: δεν έχω αυτοκίνητο (dhen ekho aftokinito), 'not I-have car'.
Αυτό (afto) is 'this one' for neuter words – it points at το τηλέφωνό μου (to tilefono mou = my phone).
'A' changes form as the object: ένας (enas) becomes έναν (enan) when the coffee is what you want – θέλω έναν καφέ (thelo enan kafe).
Masculine 'the' switches ο (o) to τον (ton) when the noun is the object: θέλουμε τον λογαριασμό (theloume ton loghariasmo).
Place names usually carry the article: για την Αθήνα (ya tin Athina) is literally 'for the Athens'.
Να (na) links verbs where English uses 'to': θέλω να πάω (thelo na pao = I want to go). Greek chains verbs with να (na), not a 'to' form.
Greek has no 'to speak' form. After θέλω you conjugate again with να: θέλω να μιλάω (thelo na milao) is literally 'I want that I speak'.
The verb after να (na) carries its own person: θέλεις να πάμε (thelis na pame) = you want US to go – πάμε (pame) already says 'us'.
'This X' keeps 'the': αυτό το βιβλίο (afto to vivlio) is literally 'this the book' – the article never drops.
'This' doesn't replace 'the' – Greek stacks them: αυτή η τσάντα (afti i tsanta) is literally 'this the bag'.
'This' agrees in gender: your aunt is feminine, so αυτή (afti). A man would be αυτός (aftos), a thing αυτό (afto).
Cities keep their article: στην Αθήνα (stin Athina) is literally 'to the Athens'. Greek place names almost always carry 'the'.
Article + adjective stands alone: θέλω το μικρό (thelo to mikro) = I want the small one. Greek has no word for 'one' here.
Τι κάνεις; (Ti kanis) on its own is the greeting 'how are you?'. Adding a topic like το πρωί (to proi = in the morning) turns it back into a real 'what do you do?'.
The accent matters: πού (pou) with an accent asks 'where'; unaccented που (pou) means 'that/which'.
'Who' matches gender: ποιος (pios) for masculine like ο γιατρός (o yatros), ποια (pia) feminine, ποιο (pio) neuter.
The accent flips the meaning: πώς (pos) asks 'how', as in πώς πας (pos pas = how do you get there); unaccented πως (pos) means 'that'.
'Which' has gender: ποια (pia) is feminine to match αδερφή (adherfi = sister). Asking about a brother, you'd switch to ποιος (pios).
Swap the little word to ask about others: πώς τον λένε (pos ton lene) is literally 'how do they call him' – what's his name.
Languages take στα (sta): στα ελληνικά (sta elliniká = in Greek), στα αγγλικά (sta angliká = in English).
Πόσο (póso) before a describing word asks 'how': πόσο μακριά; (póso makriá = how far?), πόσο μεγάλο (póso megálo = how big).
